steps.say: Three Claude models got the same brief. A two-storey beach house, every plank written in Python, that you can walk through in a browser.
These are the three files, in this site's own viewer. One was done in forty-two minutes. Which would you keep?

scenes.headline: Opus, Fable and Sonnet build the same beach house
scenes.sub: A critic loop, a baked light, and a blind judgement
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Dormer! Let's walk through all three, and see what each one cost.

stations.label: Judge
stations.sub: a fresh subagent: yes or no

steps.say: The loop is the same for all three. A Python script builds the whole scene from nothing.

steps.term: Atlas: one texture holding every surface's light
steps.say: Blender's Cycles bakes the light into textures, so the browser never computes a shadow.
Geometry and atlases go into one file of about five megabytes.
Headless Chromium screenshots it in the site's viewer.
And a brand new subagent, one that has seen nothing else, answers yes or no. Then go again.
Opus went first. Seven passes, four critics, four noes. The last one said:

steps.caption: The fourth critic
steps.say: No, but it is close.
It built the best-dressed site of the three. A dune fence, a boardwalk to a fire pit, an outdoor shower.

steps.caption: Walk mode, the living room
steps.say: And it wrote the viewer the other two were tested in.
Fable never asked Cycles for colour. It baked only the light, and painted the boards and shingles in afterwards.
Five critics: no, no, no, yes, yes. About ninety-three minutes, across three machines.

steps.caption: The rail shadows are in the baked atlas
steps.say: Out on the balcony you can see what that bought. The rail shadows are part of the texture.
Sonnet built its geometry in pure Python, before Blender ever saw it. About four thousand one hundred and sixty flat faces.
Its third critic said yes, after about forty-two minutes. The fastest yes on the page.

steps.caption: Box-modelled furniture, no bevels
steps.say: The architecture is crisp. The furniture is plain boxes.

judged: first for two of three judges

steps.say: Put the three loops on one clock. Each stamp is a critic's verdict.
Sonnet: no, no, yes.
Opus: four noes, the last one close.
Fable: three noes, then two yeses, at about twice the time.
So which house is best? A critic can't say. It only answers: is this done?

scenes.title: Eleven views, three judges, no names

steps.say: So the article ran a blind test. Eleven matched views of all three houses, shown to three fresh judges with the names removed.

steps.caption: Reveal models and ranks
steps.say: Reveal the names, and every judge's ranking is there, view by view.

states.say: Fable took seventeen first places. Opus took sixteen. Sonnet, with the fastest yes, took none.

steps.caption: From the air: Opus, all six judgements
steps.say: The split is not random. From the air, Opus won every judgement. Its site tells the story.

steps.caption: Deck and balcony: Fable, with every judge
steps.say: At eye level, where a visitor actually stands, Fable's baked light won the deck and the balcony with every judge.

scenes.text: A critic's yes means nothing is visibly broken. It does not mean the house is good.
scenes.say: A critic's yes means nothing is visibly broken. It does not mean the house is good. Rounds are what you pay for.

recap: Bake the light, draw it unlit
Fable first, Opus best from the air
scenes.say: Sonnet got the fastest yes and came last. Fable won narrowly, and Opus is best from the air. Go and walk them yourself. Thanks for watching!
